title: Ansel and the Bakery
premise: Orsen Ishikawa, a cellist whose hands froze mid-concert in front of two thousand people, returns home for the Ishikawa family reunion dreading the question of what comes next. To deflect pity, they claim to be seeing someone—Ansel, the quiet baker whose shop sits below Orsen's apartment—and the fake date becomes real by dessert. As Orsen relearns the cello in Ansel's flour-warmed kitchen, they uncover that the bakery was left to Ansel by a grandmother whose memory is slipping, and that Ansel's family intends to sell the building out from under her. When the sale closes on the same weekend as Orsen's second-chance recital, Orsen must choose between fleeing failure again and performing a piece written for Ansel's grandmother—ending with the bakery saved, the grandmother remembered, and Orsen asking Ansel to stay past the last train.
about_author: Theo Yarrow is a former pastry cook turned novelist who writes romances about people rebuilding themselves in small, warm rooms. They live above a bakery, which they insist is not where they get all their ideas, and it is exactly where they get all their ideas.

chapters.title: The Silence After
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Eight months after freezing mid-Bach in a packed concert hall, Orsen lives half-shut in the apartment above Ansel's bakery, unable to touch the cello case in the corner. The emotional beat is shame calcifying into routine—until an envelope arrives: the annual Ishikawa reunion, plus a note from their mother asking who they're bringing.

chapters.title: Flour at Six A.M.
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Unable to sleep, Orsen descends at dawn and watches Ansel work through the window—precise, unhurried, entirely absorbed. They speak for the first time in months of shared stairs. Ansel offers a warm croissant and no questions, and Orsen, starved for a place without expectations, starts coming every morning.

chapters.title: A Convenient Lie
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Cornered by a cousin's phone call, Orsen blurts that they're seeing the baker downstairs. Panic: the reunion is in three weeks, and the family will expect proof. The beat is reckless improvisation—Orsen asks Ansel to be their fake partner, framing it as a favor between strangers.

chapters.title: Terms and Conditions
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel agrees, but we learn their motive: a family reunion of their own looms, and a confident partner would deflect questions about the bakery's future. They set rules—no real feelings, no touching unless necessary. The beat is guarded hope disguised as pragmatism.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Dual POV, alternating scenes. Fake-date practice over coffee: learning each other's tells, inventing a meet-cute, arguing about whether Orsen's family will believe anyone this calm. Laughter breaks through the transaction, and both are quietly alarmed by how easy it feels.

chapters.title: Grandmother Rose
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel introduces Orsen to Grandma Rose, the bakery's founder, whose memory now loops between decades. Rose mistakes Orsen for a musician she once knew and asks them to play 'the piece' someday. Ansel deflects; Orsen notices the framed photo of a cellist on the wall—and feels the floor tilt.

chapters.title: The Letter from Meridian Holdings
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel's uncle arrives with papers: the building is being sold to a developer, and Rose's ownership was never properly transferred after her husband's death. The lease dies in sixty days. Ansel hides the letter; the beat is dread and inherited powerlessness.

chapters.title: Packing the Cello
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen opens the cello case for the first time in eight months, fingers hovering, and cannot. But that night they play a recording of Bach for Ansel in the empty bakery, and Ansel, without comment, leaves a slice of lemon cake beside them. The beat is grief beginning to thaw.

chapters.title: Arrival
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. The reunion begins at the family lake house. Orsen and Ansel arrive as a couple; the Ishikawas descend—mother's careful concern, a rival cousin's success, an aunt's probing questions. Ansel performs calm brilliantly, and Orsen watches their family through Ansel's eyes and sees its cruelty for the first time.

chapters.title: Dessert
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. At the reunion dinner, cornered by Orsen's mother, Ansel improvises a story about how they met that is too specific, too tender, to be fiction. Orsen plays along and their hands find each other under the table. The beat: the fake date turns real by dessert, exactly as promised.

chapters.title: The Boathouse
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen escapes to the boathouse; Ansel follows. Orsen confesses the frozen concert, the humiliation, the fear that their hands are broken and so are they. Ansel doesn't reassure—they listen. First real kiss. The beat is vulnerability rewarded, and terror at what that means.

chapters.title: Rules Broken
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Back in the city, Ansel tries to reinstate the rules and fails within a week. Mornings become shared; Orsen starts sketching a melody on napkins. But Ansel is still hiding the sale letter, and the chapter ends with Rose asking Ansel directly, 'Is the bakery still mine?'—and Ansel lying to her face.

chapters.title: The Piece
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen finds sheet music in the bakery's back room: an unfinished cello piece in Rose's late husband's handwriting, written for Rose, never performed. Rose, in a lucid moment, tells Orsen her husband was the cellist in the photo—and asks Orsen to finish it. The beat is inheritance as invitation.

chapters.title: Sixty Days
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Ansel finally tells Orsen about the sale. Orsen is furious—not about the lie, but that Ansel carried it alone. They fight in the flour-dusted kitchen, and the fight cracks into something honest: both of them are experts at disappearing. They agree to fight the sale together.

chapters.title: Paper Trails
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen uses their family's one useful trait—relentless research—to dig into the property records and finds a path: if Rose can be declared competent to execute a trust, the sale stalls. But it requires a public hearing where Rose must testify. The beat is fragile strategy and mounting stakes.

chapters.title: The Uncle's Offer
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The uncle offers Ansel a buyout and a bakery job in another city—security in exchange for surrender. He invokes Ansel's dead father's failures to twist the knife. Ansel almost signs. The beat is the seduction of escape, and the chapter ends with Ansel tearing the check in half.

chapters.title: Hands
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Orsen attempts the unfinished piece and their hands seize—the old terror returning at the worst moment. Ansel finds them shaking and says the thing that changes everything: 'You don't owe the hall a perfect performance. You owe Rose a finished song.' Orsen practices at dawn, badly, bravely, daily.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Rose testifies, losing and finding her thread as the room waits—until she speaks of the bakery in terms so precise and loving that the board hesitates. The trust is granted a continuance, not a victory: the sale is delayed, not dead. The beat is dignity against machinery, and a deadline now attached to everything.

chapters.title: Last Train
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. A developer counterattack: an emergency permit hearing scheduled the same night as the recital where Orsen will premiere the finished piece. Ansel tells Orsen to play and let Ansel fight alone; Orsen refuses. The beat is two people refusing to abandon each other's battles, with time visibly running out.

chapters.title: The Recital
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. A small hall, Rose in the front row, the Ishikawas in the back. Orsen's hands tremble on the first note—and hold. They perform Rose's husband's finished piece as Ansel slips out mid-concert to the permit hearing, phone livestreaming the music into the room. The beat is triumph braided with absence.

chapters.title: What Rose Built
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. At the hearing, the developer's own architect—moved by the music and by Rose's testimony—reveals the building qualifies for heritage protection. The sale collapses. Ansel runs back through the rain to the hall and arrives as the last note fades. The beat is the fight won by the thing they were protecting all along.

chapters.title: After the Last Train
chapters.summary: Orsen's POV. Epilogue, months later. The bakery has Rose's name restored above the door; Orsen teaches cello in the back room on Sundays. On the platform after a late concert, Orsen asks Ansel to come home instead of catching the last train. Ansel stays. The beat is quiet, chosen permanence—second chances, it turns out, are for people who finally show up.
